## Introduction (preview)

Fair warning. This is an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack, and any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously.

This preview drops you into the middle of the book. Part Three. It's called C Things That Looked Like A Things.

Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work. The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing.

And from the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. The applause is loud, and the real work is quieter. This book is about that gap, between what people saw and what was really going on.

A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. The richer guy, the more experienced, the wisest. The better father, the better brother, the better sister, the better daughter.

The Valley falls in love with products. Specific wins, in specific years. I got more out of building a platform: a foundation you can stand on, then build the next thing on, and the thing after that. You don't invent a career in one move. You stack building blocks: habits, fundamentals, the unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. That layer is what you actually stand on later.

It's all relative, how good you look from the outside. But one thing stayed for certain. I just kept going. And I kept doing my best.

Then the work itself changed. I'm usually the most excited person in the room about AI. Which is funny, because I should be the saddest. Because AI came after the code writers first. In my own work, AI now writes essentially all of the code I ship. That's how I work. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure.

Software engineering was never about writing code. Writing code was just the tedious part you had to do to build your ideas. It's about solving big problems with abstraction. Each part is just data in, some logic, and data out. Abstraction is key. You climb down the ladder, and you climb back up.

So software engineering practices have to be geared around that. That's what Software Engineering 101 and 201 are about, and it's the second half of this book: how to work now, and how companies should use AI.

The book begins with a green-screen dream, and it ends by dreaming about AI. This part, in the middle, is the turn. It's free. It's open. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. The story is still being written.

## From the back cover

An embellished fictional dramatization about C players, the gap between applause and the work, and platforms you can actually stand on. A free OpenBook, like open-source software.

This preview is from the middle of the book: Part Three, C Things That Looked Like A Things, and the turn that follows. The Valley tells a story about A players. The real work looks like another Tuesday.

The second half is about how to work now that, in Clark's own work, AI writes essentially all of the code he ships — his workflow, not a measured team result or a general industry figure — and how companies should use it.

Silicon Valley C Players. Written and interviewed by AI, from Clark Huang's own words. Coming in 2027.

## Lessons

### AI Tips

Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/index.md

- Lesson 1: [Paste First, Ask Second](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/01-paste-first-ask-second/index.md) — When an AI gives you a useless answer, it is usually not the AI's fault: you described the problem instead of showing it. Without the real material, it can only guess. Paste the screenshot, document, error message, or email thread first, and the same question gets a specific, usable answer.
  - Rule: Paste first, ask second. Hand over the screenshot, document, error message, or email thread before you type a single word of your question.
- Lesson 2: [Ask for Proof, Not “Done”](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/02-ask-for-proof/index.md) — When a bot says “done”, it is usually reporting the status of the step it ran, not whether the outcome you wanted is true. Five short examples show the gap, and none of them is a bot misbehaving. The fix is to ask for something only a real result can produce.
  - Rule: Ask for the artifact, not the status: the ticket numbers, a screenshot on the actual device, counts per item instead of a job status, a link you can click yourself. No artifact means it hasn't happened yet.
- Lesson 3: [Define the Number Before You Ask for It](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/03-define-the-number-before-you-ask-for-it/index.md) — Ask a bot for a number with a loose word in it and it will quietly pick a meaning, then hand you a confident, wrong answer. This tip shows how one word like "got" or "orders" can mean several populations, and the one extra sentence that removes the guess.
  - Rule: Before asking any agent or analyst for a number, state three things: the exact metric (which event, which status), the source system your team signs off on, and the as-of date. Where you can, add a number you already know ("this should land near X, tell me if it doesn't") so the answer has to reconcile. If a vague question gets a fast, confident answer, treat that speed as the warning sign and ask what interpretation was used.
- Lesson 4: [Know What the Bot Can Actually Reach](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/04-know-what-the-bot-can-actually-reach/index.md) — A bot's usefulness is bounded by what it's connected to, and it almost never tells you where that boundary is. Five generic examples show how a missing link, an unread thread reply or a doc it can't write turns into something that sounds like success.
  - Rule: Before handing a bot a task, confirm which bot you're talking to and what it's connected to. Treat any "I'll write / file / run / log it" as a claim about access, not a status, and check it can actually do that. Remember that an approval, a chat request to borrow access, or an untagged thread reply doesn't grant access or reach the bot. Access is granted where the tool is administered.
- Lesson 5: [Don't Trust "I Can't"](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/05-dont-trust-i-cant/index.md) — A bot's "I can't" is often a prediction, not a test. It hasn't tried, or it guessed at your role. This tip shows how to tell a soft refusal from a real limit, so you push on the right ones and never around a genuine guardrail.
  - Rule: When an agent says it can't, check whether it names the missing piece. A bare refusal: ask it to find another permitted route and try before saying no. A named blocker (a key, an account link, someone's approval): ask it to confirm it actually checked, and if it holds, go get that piece rather than arguing. Ask for the goal, not the method, state your role and access up front, pre-authorise a second attempt, and ask for the exact step that stopped it. "Find a way" never means working around a real limit.
- Lesson 6: [Teach It Once](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/06-teach-it-once/index.md) — Knowledge is what a bot has picked up. Skills are jobs you've written down for it. This tip shows how to save what a bot works out so nobody repeats it, why a good skill is mostly guardrails, and how saved rules can fence a credential that does more than the job needs.
  - Rule: When you explain the same thing to a bot a second time, or it finally gets something right after getting it wrong, have it save the rule. Write skills mostly as boundaries: when to act, when not to, whose data, where to report, what to do when unsure, and when to stop. Where a credential can do more than the job needs, add an explicit rule (e.g. reads only, no writes without approval), but treat it as a seatbelt, not a vault, and use a narrower credential for anything that genuinely matters.
- Lesson 7: [The Second Message](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/07-the-second-message/index.md) — Most people read the first answer and stop. Either they settle for it or give up on the tool. One follow-up line in the same chat usually turns a generic draft into a usable one, and asking the A.I. to interview you first is better still.
  - Rule: Treat the first answer as a draft, not a verdict. Reply in the same conversation with one of three follow-ups: say specifically what's wrong, ask for a different shape, or give it something concrete to work from. For anything you'll care about, start by telling it: "Before you write it, ask me what you need to know." Don't open a new chat to fix a draft, because that throws away the context it has built.
- Lesson 8: [Stop Re-Explaining Yourself](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/08-stop-re-explaining-yourself/index.md) — If every Claude chat starts with you re-explaining your job and re-attaching the same file, a Project fixes it: shared knowledge and instructions in one place. This tip covers what sharing a project hands over (and what stays private), the permission choices, and where Cowork tasks run.
  - Rule: When you find yourself re-uploading the same files or repeating the same instructions, put them in a Claude Project: files in project knowledge, standing rules in project instructions. Share the project with the people who'd benefit. Sharing hands over knowledge and instructions, while each person's chats stay private unless they share one deliberately. Choose org-wide or invite-only, and can-view or can-edit. If a task "can't see" your local folder, check whether it needs the desktop app open.
- Lesson 9: [Claude Code Isn't Just for Developers](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/09-claude-code-isnt-just-for-developers/index.md) — Claude Code's name keeps most non-developers away, but it works on any folder of ordinary files, driven by plain-English requests. This tip shows what it can do with screenshots, invoices and transcripts, what "it's a terminal" really means, and how to start in five minutes.
  - Rule: For any job that means reading, renaming, or pulling information across many files in one folder, try Claude Code before doing it by hand: install it, point it at the folder, and describe the outcome in plain English. Use Esc to interrupt, /help to see what it can do, and the desktop app if you'd rather not use a terminal. Check the result before relying on it.
- Lesson 10: [The Label Is Not the Definition](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/10-the-label-is-not-the-definition/index.md) — The most common mistake in six weeks of bots' self-written lessons: trusting what a field is called instead of what it counts. A number with the wrong definition still ties out and reconciles, so nothing looks wrong and it travels.
  - Rule: Before using or explaining a number, find out what it actually counts. Read the definition, not the field name. Treat a surprising number as a likely definition problem before treating it as a story. When the source is unclear, ask the data owner which table holds the number they actually sign off on, and say which dataset every reported number came from.
- Lesson 11: [Your Bot in the Meeting](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/11-your-bot-in-the-meeting/index.md) — A notetaker records one call and summarises it. A bot that's connected to your team's work can answer questions live, turn action items into real tickets, and remember what was decided last week. This tip shows how to try it on one meeting, and the limit that catches people out.
  - Rule: Try a connected team bot on one recurring meeting, the one where someone always says "I'll check and get back to you." Invite it (or give it the link) and admit it from the waiting room. Afterwards, if you invited it, share the notes yourself, because often only the inviter receives them. Expect a first version: it may not see screen shares or speak aloud yet.
- Lesson 12: [Brief the Next Chat](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/12-brief-the-next-chat/index.md) — Long chats drift without warning: early decisions count for less and can fall out of view. When a chat gets long, have it write a handoff and carry on in a fresh chat.
  - Rule: When a chat gets long, brief the next one: the goal and the limits, every decision so far, what's still open, and read it before you paste it.
- Lesson 13: [Open the Source](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/13-open-the-source/index.md) — AI-supplied citations can be perfectly formatted and completely invented, and pushed on a dead link a model may insist the page changed. A reference you haven't opened is a claim, not a source.
  - Rule: Open it before you use it: click the link, check the title and authors, find the sentence you need on the page. Nothing to open? Not a source yet.
- Lesson 14: [Ask It to Disagree](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/14-ask-it-to-disagree/index.md) — Models lean toward the view already in your question, so a yes to a leading question isn't a second opinion. Ask for the case against before you ask for advice: a review, not a fight.
  - Rule: Ask for the case against: leave your answer out of the question, ask for the strongest case against and how you could be wrong, then ask what it recommends.
- Lesson 15: [Treat Memory Like Notes](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/15-treat-memory-like-notes/index.md) — AI memory is a small set of saved notes, not a mind. Notes can be never saved, saved wrong, off-topic or stale, and they won't keep up unless you update them.
  - Rule: Treat memory like notes: say what matters in the prompt, don't assume a new chat knows, read your memory now and then, and fix or delete what's wrong.
- Lesson 16: [Don't Fire and Forget](https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/16-dont-fire-and-forget/index.md) — Agents act on real systems, and a rule typed into a prompt is not a lock. Put the lock in access and approval settings, and keep the judgment for steps you can't undo.
  - Rule: Set the stop before you start: say what done looks like, limit what it can touch, require approval before delete, reset, push or send, and watch the first few steps.

### Software Engineering 101

Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/index.md

- Lesson 1: [Plan, Build, Verify (and When to Skip It)](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/01-plan-build-verify/index.md) — How do you fix code you don't understand when you only get one shot? Split the work into four roles: a person who owns the problem, a planner, a builder, and a verifier on a different model that can only read and report. Loop until the verifier runs out of serious things to say. Then: what that costs, and when a lighter path is good enough.
  - Rule: If a change can't be rolled back, and the person asking can't check it themselves, it gets an independent review, on a different model, before it ships. That's the floor. The longer list, of when to use the full pattern, is judgment.
- Lesson 2: [Rigor Follows Risk](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/02-rigor-follows-risk/index.md) — A patch in ten minutes or the root cause in two days? Redeploy speed is only half the question: a redeploy fixes the code, but it doesn't undo what the code did. Product shape is uncertain and easy to change, so ship it rough behind a flag. Correctness you can't undo, meaning money, customer data, and messages, gets the root cause.
  - Rule: Rough is fine for product shape. It is never fine for money, customer data, or anything that can't be undone. If a piece of work is both, the stricter standard wins. For that kind of work: stop any live damage first, then find the root cause, and give the estimate in usage, not in days.
- Lesson 3: [Principles Over Languages](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/03-principles-over-languages/index.md) — Why a computer science education built on ideas, not languages, still pays off, and why it matters more now that agents write the syntax.
  - Rule: When you make a design choice, explain the principle behind it, in plain words. Not just the framework feature you used.
- Lesson 4: [The Abstraction Ladder](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/04-abstraction-ladder/index.md) — AI coding is one more rung on a ladder that runs from logic gates up. Stay at the top, and know when to send your agent down a rung.
  - Rule: Break a task into small pieces that each do one thing. And when something on one layer doesn't add up, look at the layer below, before you change anything.
- Lesson 5: [Understand Before You Change](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/05-understand-before-you-change/index.md) — A perfect fix for the wrong problem is still wrong. Own the problem, restate it, reproduce and trace it, then fix the cause.
  - Rule: Before planning, restate the problem in plain words, and confirm it with the person who gave you the task. They own the problem. Before fixing, reproduce it if you can, and trace what actually happens. Then fix the cause, not the symptom.
- Lesson 6: [Say What, Not How](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/06-say-what-not-how/index.md) — Like a database optimizer, an agent does its best work when you state the outcome and the limits, not the steps. Too tight and too loose both cost you.
  - Rule: A spec states the outcome, and what must not break. It doesn't dictate steps, unless a step is itself a requirement. And before you start the work, give a cost forecast.
- Lesson 7: [Old Patterns, New Clothes](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/07-old-patterns-new-clothes/index.md) — Pair programming, test-first and code review still work with agents in the seats. Cheaper tests change the trade, and three anti-patterns to watch for.
  - Rule: Write the failing test before the fix. No bug fix merges without a test that would have caught the bug. And the agent that wrote the code never approves it.
- Lesson 8: [Agile at Agent Speed](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/08-agile-at-agent-speed/index.md) — Keep every scrum ceremony, but run the loop daily. Deploy continuously, ship features switched off behind a flag, and write down what you learned.
  - Rule: Ship small changes continuously, once the automated checks pass. New features ship switched off, behind a flag. A person decides when each one turns on, for one client or a small group first. And end every session with a short written note on what was learned.
- Lesson 9: [Know What It Costs](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/09-know-what-it-costs/index.md) — AI usage is the new currency of software. See the spend, the limit and a priced forecast before you start, and remember that owning software costs more than building it.
  - Rule: Before any sizable task, show the spend so far, the limit, and a forecast for each path. If you can't see a number, say so, and label an estimate as an estimate. Afterward, record what it actually cost. And before you build something new, check what already exists.
- Lesson 10: [Strict About Data, Relaxed About the Perimeter](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/10-strict-about-data/index.md) — Be uncompromising about customer personal data and card data, pragmatic about where internal apps live, and see the whole series on one screen.
  - Rule: Never store, log, or send raw card data. Customer personal data stays out of logs, errors, test data, and your own working notes. Internal apps sit behind company sign-in, on every route. And any change that touches personal data or payments gets an independent review.

### Software Engineering 201

Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/index.md

- Lesson 1: [Four Eras of Building Systems](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/01-four-eras-of-building-systems/index.md) — How we build big systems has changed from thirty, twenty and ten years ago to now, with agents doing much of the building. One useful lens is that architecture bends around whatever is scarcest. Machines were scarce in the mid-1990s, coordination in the 2000s, and seeing the whole system in the 2010s. Now the scarce things are knowing the work is right and how much of the system an agent can see at once. So design for checking: clear module boundaries, one repository an agent can read, tests and specs it can run, and decisions written down. This is where the thinking is heading, not a settled answer. Four things never changed: the data model outlives the code, money has to add up, you depend on things you don't control, and someone has to understand the layer below.
  - Rule: Before you design a system, write down four things: where the boundaries are, what the data model is, what you depend on but don't control, and how you'll know it's right. Put that note in the repository, where every agent and person working on the system can read it, and keep it current as the design changes.
- Lesson 2: [Build the Whole System, AI-Native](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/02-build-the-whole-system-ai-native/index.md) — After the four eras, the first step from one loop to enterprise systems: what changes when you build a whole app or system with AI instead of one fix. A system is AI-native when agents and people can both read it, navigate it, contribute to it, and rebuild it. That takes four things: a Markdown twin, an index, and an AGENTS.md for every part; specs and briefs as the source; tests and checks as the contract; and staging plus a person's approval before anything reaches production. The worked example is this site, and the same four things matter even more at enterprise scale.
  - Rule: Before you build anything bigger than one fix, make it readable to agents and people: a Markdown twin for every page, an index of the whole system, and an AGENTS.md that says how to work there. Treat specs and briefs as the source and tests and checks as the contract, and send every change through staging for a person to approve before it reaches production.
- Lesson 3: [Decompose the System into a Graph](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/03-decompose-the-system-into-a-graph/index.md) — An enterprise system is too big for one loop, so draw it as a graph. A numbered plan only shows the order someone wrote the steps in; the test for any two steps is what crosses between them, and “and then” is not a dependency. The worked example is this site: four parts that share one generator, and one lesson's build, a strict chain that forks after the render. The graph decides which loops exist and which can run at the same time, and every part still gets its own plan, build, and verify loop. An earlier recording of this material, made when it was lesson 1, is at https://clarkhuang.github.io/videos/se201-01-from-loop-to-graph.mp4.
  - Rule: Before any job with more than one part, draw the graph. Name the parts, and give each one a boundary and an owner. Draw an arrow only where something crosses from one part to another; “and then” is not a dependency. Anything two parts share becomes its own node, with one owner. Run the parts with no arrow between them at the same time, and give every part its own plan, build, and verify loop, with its own finish line and its own check.
- Lesson 4: [Parallel Agents, One Integration](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/04-parallel-agents-one-integration/index.md) — Three agents can each pass their own check while the system is still broken, because no check has seen the parts together. Parallel work is only fast if it comes back together cleanly, so plan the integration first: a shared contract written before the work starts, one merge point used early, and tests on the whole system. The worked example is Software Engineering 101, lessons 3 to 5: built at the same time, then brought together through one shared script format, one content file, and one generator, and shipped in one change. Today the same path adds a whole-site check and a pull request to staging that a person approves.
  - Rule: Before you run agents in parallel, plan how the work comes back together. Write the shared contract first: the interfaces, the formats, the names, and who owns which files; when it has to change, change it in one place. Give each agent its own brief, its own finish line, and its own check, and make matching the contract part of that check. Merge early, in one place, and test the whole system, not just each part. If two parts keep needing each other's answers, they are not parallel work: go back to the graph.
- Lesson 5: [Governance: Where People Decide](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/05-governance-where-people-decide/index.md) — Every era had a place where a person said yes: a change board signing off a whole release, then a teammate reviewing the code, then an approval on a pull request. Each was sized for people writing the code, so when agents write changes faster than anyone can read them all, that place has to be designed, not inherited. A good rule of thumb is four questions: does it move money, touch customer data, is it hard to undo, or is it a judgment call no check can make? One yes and a named person decides; four no's and that kind of change can ship on its checks. The worked example is a made-up subscription-billing system, where six pieces of an agent's work lead to four stops and two changes that never wait, and where the agent prepares each decision: what changes, why, the evidence, the risk, and the way back. Write down who approves what in the repository, let the pipeline enforce it, and start strict, releasing one kind of change at a time as its checks earn trust.
  - Rule: Before a change ships, find out who decides. Money, customer data, hard to undo, or a judgment call that no check can make: stop for the person named in the repo, and bring the change, the evidence, the risk, and the way back. Not on the list? Stop and ask. Ship on checks alone only what a person has released. In full: bring the decision ready to make (what changes, why, the evidence, the risk, and the way back), and don't classify or approve your own change.
- Lesson 6: [Quality, Feedback, and Observability](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/06-quality-feedback-and-observability/index.md) — A green build says the code did what its tests asked; it says nothing about what happened last night. Ten years ago the scarce thing was seeing the whole system, and logs, metrics and traces answered "what happened?". Now the scarce thing is knowing it's right, and no dashboard can answer that until someone has written down what right means. The worked example is a made-up subscription-billing system: "every renewal charged the right amount, exactly once" becomes three checks, and running them on last night's renewals finds three wrong ones inside totals that match exactly. Write the check once and run it twice, before a change ships and after every run; make every step leave a record that people and agents can both read; and feed every miss back into the brief and the checks, while a person still reads a sample, because a check only catches what somebody thought to ask.
  - Rule: Before you build, write down what right means, as checks you can run, in the business's words. Run them before a change ships, and after every run. Leave a record at every step. When a check fails, stop and tell a person. Feed every miss back into the brief and the checks. In full: run the checks on samples before a change ships and on the real data after every run, leave each record in a shape people and agents can both read, and let every miss make the next run better.
- Lesson 7: [Skills as Building Blocks](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/07-skills-as-building-blocks/index.md) — Three capable agents can do the same job three different ways when nobody wrote down how. Software has had several units of reuse: libraries, frameworks, then services behind an API. A skill reuses something different: how a job gets done. The worked example is a made-up subscription-billing system and the job of adding a plan or a price: the skill is one page saying when to use it, the inputs, the steps, the checks, and the traps. It is a runbook; what has changed is the reader, an agent that reads it on every run and guesses wherever the page is silent. So keep it in the repository, test it with a fresh agent, and when a run goes wrong, fix the skill so every later run gets the fix.
  - Rule: When a job comes back a third time, write it as a skill: when to use it, inputs, steps, checks, and traps. Keep it in the repo, and test it with a fresh agent. When a run goes wrong, fix the skill, not just the run. In full: write it sooner if a mistake costs money. If an input is missing, ask instead of guessing, and if a check fails, stop and say so. Make any step that needs no judgment a script the skill calls. Keep the skill versioned and reviewed like code, and test it by handing it to a fresh agent that has never seen the job.
- Lesson 8: [Routines, Pipelines, and Integration](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/08-routines-pipelines-and-integration/index.md) — A job charges a card, the answer is lost, and the job tries again: unless someone designed that retry to be safe, the customer can be charged twice. Connecting systems is the oldest problem in this series, from overnight batch files and EDI, to web services, to an API for everything, to agents calling tools, and all of them are still running somewhere. Some work should start on its own: call a skill plus a trigger a routine, and routines chained together a pipeline. The worked example is the nightly billing run of a made-up subscription-billing system: a clear format at every hand-off, a record from every step whose counts add up, a retry made safe with an idempotency key, and a reconcile step that tells a person when the numbers don't match. The same thinking covers a partner's file that arrives late, twice, or broken: design for at least once, and make twice harmless.
  - Rule: Before any work runs on its own, write down four things: what starts it, what crosses at each hand-off, what record each step leaves, and what happens when a step fails, or runs twice. No answer? It isn't ready to run unattended. In full: give every hand-off a clear, written format. Make every step leave a record that adds up, and make every step safe to run twice. When the numbers don't match, don't guess and don't fix them quietly: keep every record and tell a person. Keep that note where the agents and people who run the work can read it.
- Lesson 9: [Agents That Operate Enterprise Systems](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/09-agents-that-operate-enterprise-systems/index.md) (outline) — Agents that run the system, not just build it, with identity, least access, and an audit trail. The last step before the capstone: agents that operate enterprise systems day to day. Give each agent a clear job, its own identity, and the least access it needs, so every action is permitted, logged, and auditable. Picture a payments or investment system where an agent reconciles accounts overnight and flags anything that doesn't add up, while a person approves anything that moves money. Keep secrets and customer data out of reach, keep people at the decision points, and remember that you still own the outcome. Lesson 10, the capstone, puts all nine lessons to work on one small feature.
- Lesson 10: [Capstone: One Feature, End to End](https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/10-capstone-one-feature-end-to-end/index.md) — The capstone builds one small feature of a made-up subscription-billing system end to end, using every lesson in the series in order: a customer on a $30 monthly plan switches to a $300 annual plan ten days into the month. What to charge depends on a rule nobody has written down, so the plan comes first: say what right means and let a person set the rule; put it in a spec in the repository; draw the graph and find the one new thing that crosses, the quote; make the quote's format the shared contract for three agents and one merge point; name who decides; turn "right" into three checks that run before the change ships and every night after; and notice that adding a plan is already a skill. Then the plan is carried out: the parts are built at the same time, the finance owner says yes, the feature runs as a pipeline with an idempotency key on the charge, and an agent with its own identity and read-only access works the nightly reconcile, flags a double charge for a person to refund, and the miss becomes a fourth check. Under all of it, the four constants from lesson 1 still hold.
  - Rule: Before you build a whole feature, write the plan in the repo, and show a person. What right means, as checks. The graph, and the shared contract. Who decides. What's already a skill. What runs on its own, and under whose identity. A blank line? Stop, and ask. In full: before you build a feature with more than one part, write the plan in the repository, show it to a person, and wait for a yes. The plan says: what right means, as checks you can run before the change ships and after every run; the graph of the parts, the contract they share, and the one place they merge; who decides, by name or role, and what you will bring them; which parts are already a skill; and what will run on its own, what starts it, what happens when a step fails or runs twice, and under whose identity and access it runs. If you cannot fill in a line, do not guess: stop, and ask.
